title: Architecture in Python
summary: Layers, ports and adapters, repositories, services and events: structure an application so each part can be tested alone.

lessons.title: Layers and import direction
lessons.body:
# Layers and import direction

An application grows in layers. The domain holds the business rules, the service layer runs use cases, and adapters talk to databases, files and networks. One rule keeps them apart: outer layers may import inner ones, never the reverse.

When the domain imports a database adapter, every test of a business rule needs that database, and a change of storage ripples into the rules. Keep the domain importing only the standard library and itself.

## Checking the direction

Python resolves imports while the code runs, so nothing stops a wrong one. A test can: parse each module with `ast`, collect what it imports, and compare the layers.

```python
import ast

source = ("import json\n"
          "from adapters.db import save")
tree = ast.parse(source)
for node in ast.walk(tree):
    if isinstance(node, ast.Import):
        print([a.name for a in node.names])
    if isinstance(node, ast.ImportFrom):
        print(node.module)
```

Tools such as import-linter run the same kind of check in CI.
lessons.task: Write `imported_modules(source)` returning the sorted, unique module names a source imports (`import a.b` and `from a.b import c` both give `"a.b"`; relative imports are ignored). Write `violations(modules, layers)`: `modules` maps names like `"domain.orders"` to source text, `layers` lists layer names from innermost to outermost, and the result is a sorted list of `(module, imported)` pairs where a module imports from a layer further out than its own.

checks.name: plain imports
checks.code:
got = imported_modules("import json\nimport domain.orders as orders\nimport json")
assert got == ["domain.orders", "json"], got

checks.name: from imports
checks.code:
got = imported_modules("from adapters.db import save\nfrom . import helpers\nfrom .models import X")
assert got == ["adapters.db"], got

checks.name: an outward import is flagged
checks.code:
layers = ["domain", "service", "adapters"]
modules = {
    "domain.orders": "from adapters.db import save",
    "adapters.db": "import domain.orders",
}
got = violations(modules, layers)
assert got == [("domain.orders", "adapters.db")], got

checks.name: inward and outside imports are fine
checks.code:
layers = ["domain", "service", "adapters"]
modules = {
    "service.place_order": "import json\nfrom domain.orders import Order",
    "service.refund": "from service.place_order import place",
    "domain.money": "from decimal import Decimal",
}
got = violations(modules, layers)
assert got == [], got

checks.name: imports inside functions count

hints: `ast.walk(ast.parse(source))` visits every node, including imports inside functions. There are two node types to handle: `ast.Import` and `ast.ImportFrom`.
`ast.Import` has `names`, aliases with a `.name`; `ast.ImportFrom` has `module` and `level`, which is above 0 for relative imports. A module's layer is the index of its first dotted part in `layers`.
Skip imports whose first part is not a layer. A pair is a violation when the imported layer's index is greater than the importer's: `other > own`.
lessons.explanation:
The starter flagged every import between layers, including the healthy ones that point inward, and it missed `from` imports, the most common kind. Direction is what matters: an adapter importing the domain is the design working, and the domain importing an adapter is the design leaking.

Run a check like this as a test, and the rule survives the next refactor, when nobody remembers it. Because it works on source text, it costs nothing to run and needs no imports to succeed.

lessons.title: Functional core, imperative shell
lessons.body:
# Functional core, imperative shell

Code that decides and code that does are easier to test apart. Put the decisions in pure functions that take values and return values: the functional core. Put reading, writing and printing in a thin layer around it: the imperative shell.

```python
from pathlib import Path

def word_counts(text):
    counts = {}
    for w in text.lower().split():
        counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1
    return counts

def main(path):
    text = Path(path).read_text()
    for w, n in word_counts(text).items():
        print(w, n)

text = "to be or not to be"
Path("a.txt").write_text(text)
main("a.txt")
```

`word_counts` needs no files and no mocks: a test passes a string and compares a dict. The shell has almost no logic, so one end-to-end test covers it.

## Plans instead of actions

When the core has to cause effects, let it return a description of them, such as a list of `("copy", name)` tuples, and let the shell carry them out. The decision becomes data you can assert on.
lessons.task: Write a pure `plan_sync(source, target)`, where both map file names to contents, returning `("copy", name)` for names only in `source`, `("update", name)` where contents differ and `("delete", name)` for names only in `target`, sorted by name. Write the shell `sync(src_dir, dst_dir)` that reads the files of both folders, carries out the plan in `dst_dir` and returns it.

checks.name: copies and deletes
checks.code:
got = plan_sync({"a.txt": "1"}, {"b.txt": "2"})
assert got == [("copy", "a.txt"), ("delete", "b.txt")], got

checks.name: updates only what changed
checks.code:
got = plan_sync({"a.txt": "1", "b.txt": "2"}, {"a.txt": "1", "b.txt": "3"})
assert got == [("update", "b.txt")], got
assert plan_sync({"a.txt": "1"}, {"a.txt": "1"}) == [], "identical folders need no actions"

checks.name: the plan is sorted by name
checks.code:
got = plan_sync({"c": "", "a": ""}, {"b": ""})
assert got == [("copy", "a"), ("delete", "b"), ("copy", "c")], got

checks.name: the shell syncs real folders
checks.code:
from pathlib import Path
src, dst = Path("shell_src"), Path("shell_dst")
src.mkdir()
dst.mkdir()
(src / "a.txt").write_text("new")
(src / "b.txt").write_text("same")
(dst / "b.txt").write_text("same")
(dst / "c.txt").write_text("old")
got = sync("shell_src", "shell_dst")
assert got == [("copy", "a.txt"), ("delete", "c.txt")], got
files = {p.name: p.read_text() for p in dst.iterdir()}
assert files == {"a.txt": "new", "b.txt": "same"}, files

checks.name: a second sync has nothing to do
checks.code:
from pathlib import Path
src, dst = Path("again_src"), Path("again_dst")
src.mkdir()
dst.mkdir()
(src / "a.txt").write_text("v2")
(dst / "a.txt").write_text("v1")
got = sync(src, dst)
assert got == [("update", "a.txt")], got
assert (dst / "a.txt").read_text() == "v2", (dst / "a.txt").read_text()
got = sync(src, dst)
assert got == [], got

hints: Build the plan from the two dicts alone: no `Path`, no `open`. Walk over every name that appears in either dict, in sorted order.
`source.keys() | target.keys()` is the union of names. Missing from `target` means copy, missing from `source` means delete, and different contents mean update.
In `sync`, read each folder into `{p.name: p.read_text()}`, call `plan_sync`, then for each action either `unlink()` the file in `dst_dir` or write the source text into it, and return the actions.
lessons.explanation:
The tangled version was only as correct as someone had checked by hand with real folders, and it forgot deletions, which is easy to miss when every test needs files on disk. With the decisions in `plan_sync`, each rule is a one-line test on two dicts.

The shell is now so plain that a single folder-to-folder test covers it. The split works at every scale: a web handler parses a request, calls the core, and turns what comes back into a response.

lessons.title: Dependency inversion
lessons.task: Write a protocol `Mailer` with `send(to, subject)`, a `FakeMailer` that appends `(to, subject)` tuples to its `.sent` list, and `Signup(mailer)` whose `register(email)` lowercases the email, raises `ValueError` if it is already registered, and otherwise stores it and sends it the subject `"Welcome"`.

checks.name: Mailer is a protocol
checks.code:
import typing
assert typing.is_protocol(Mailer), "Mailer should subclass typing.Protocol"
members = typing.get_protocol_members(Mailer)
assert members == frozenset({"send"}), members

checks.name: the welcome goes through the mailer it was given
checks.code:
mailer = FakeMailer()
signup = Signup(mailer)
signup.register("Ada@Example.org")
assert mailer.sent == [("ada@example.org", "Welcome")], mailer.sent

checks.name: any object with send fits
duplicates are refused before sending
checks.code:
mailer = FakeMailer()
signup = Signup(mailer)
signup.register("cy@example.org")
raised = False
try:
    signup.register("CY@example.org")
except ValueError:
    raised = True
assert raised, "a second registration of the same email should raise ValueError"
assert len(mailer.sent) == 1, mailer.sent

checks.name: services do not share state
checks.code:
first, second = Signup(FakeMailer()), Signup(FakeMailer())
first.register("di@example.org")
second.register("di@example.org")
assert second.mailer.sent == [("di@example.org", "Welcome")], second.mailer.sent

hints: `Signup` should not create its mailer. Take it as an `__init__` argument and keep it on `self`.
`FakeMailer` needs only `self.sent = []` and a `send` that appends a tuple. It does not inherit from `Mailer`: having the method is the contract.
In `register`: `email = email.lower()`, `if email in self.emails: raise ValueError(...)`, then add it and call `self.mailer.send(email, "Welcome")`.
lessons.explanation:
With `SmtpMailer()` built inside `__init__`, no test could see what was sent without patching the class by name. Taking the mailer as an argument turns that hidden dependency into a parameter, and a test simply passes a fake and reads its `sent` list.

The protocol is written from the service's point of view: one method, in the words the service uses. Small interfaces owned by the caller are easy to fake and hard to misuse.

lessons.title: Entities and value objects
lessons.task: Write a frozen dataclass `Money(cents, currency)` that raises `ValueError` for negative cents or a currency that is not three capital letters, adds only to the same currency (else `ValueError`), and has `split(n)` returning `n` amounts that add up to the original, differ by at most one cent, largest first. Write an entity `Account(number, owner)` whose `balance` starts at `Money(0, "EUR")`, with `deposit(money)` and equality and hashing by `number` only.

checks.name: money is a value
checks.code:
import dataclasses
assert Money(5, "EUR") == Money(5, "EUR"), "equal values should be equal"
assert len({Money(5, "EUR"), Money(5, "EUR")}) == 1, "equal values should hash alike"
frozen = False
try:
    Money(5, "EUR").cents = 6
except dataclasses.FrozenInstanceError:
    frozen = True
assert frozen, "Money should be frozen"

checks.name: money validates itself
adding money
checks.code:
got = Money(250, "EUR") + Money(100, "EUR")
assert got == Money(350, "EUR"), got
raised = False
try:
    Money(1, "EUR") + Money(1, "USD")
except ValueError:
    raised = True
assert raised, "adding EUR to USD should raise ValueError"

checks.name: split keeps every cent
checks.code:
got = Money(100, "EUR").split(3)
assert got == [Money(34, "EUR"), Money(33, "EUR"), Money(33, "EUR")], got
assert Money(7, "USD").split(1) == [Money(7, "USD")], Money(7, "USD").split(1)
parts = Money(1001, "EUR").split(4)
assert sum(p.cents for p in parts) == 1001, parts

checks.name: accounts compare by number
checks.code:
a = Account("A-1", "Ada")
b = Account("A-1", "Bo")
a.deposit(Money(500, "EUR"))
assert a == b, "the same number means the same account"
assert len({a, b}) == 1, "accounts should hash by number"
assert a != Account("A-2", "Ada"), "different numbers are different accounts"

checks.name: deposits change the balance
checks.code:
account = Account("B-7", "Cy")
assert account.balance == Money(0, "EUR"), account.balance
account.deposit(Money(500, "EUR"))
account.deposit(Money(25, "EUR"))
assert account.balance == Money(525, "EUR"), account.balance

hints: `@dataclass(frozen=True)` gives equality, hashing and immutability by value. Validation goes in `__post_init__`.
For `split`, `divmod(self.cents, n)` gives the share and the remainder; the first `remainder` parts get one extra cent.

`Account` is a plain class: `__eq__` returns `isinstance(other, Account) and other.number == self.number`, and `__hash__` returns `hash(self.number)`. Deposit by replacing `self.balance` with `self.balance + money`.
lessons.explanation:
A dataclass compares every field, so in the starter the same account with two different balances was two unequal objects, and a set of accounts could hold one account twice. Entities need identity equality, written by hand.

Values are the opposite. Freezing them means a `Money` passed around can never change under someone's feet, and validating in `__post_init__` means an invalid one can never exist. Whole cents and `divmod` keep every cent accounted for, which floats cannot promise.

lessons.title: A state machine for a workflow
lessons.body:
# A state machine for a workflow

An order moves from draft to submitted to paid to shipped, and can be cancelled until it is paid. Status checks scattered through the code drift apart. Writing the allowed moves down in one table makes the workflow explicit, easy to test and easy to draw.

```python
MOVES = {
    ("draft", "submit"): "submitted",
    ("submitted", "pay"): "paid",
    ("paid", "ship"): "shipped",
}

def step(state, action):
    if (state, action) not in MOVES:
        msg = f"no {action} from {state}"
        raise ValueError(msg)
    return MOVES[(state, action)]

state = step("draft", "submit")
print(state, step(state, "pay"))
```

The order keeps its current state, and every change goes through one method that consults the table. A list of past states gives you an audit trail for free.

## States as an Enum

Make the states an `Enum`. A typo such as `Status.PAYED` then fails at once, where a misspelt string would quietly create a new state.
lessons.task: Write an `Enum` `Status` with `DRAFT`, `SUBMITTED`, `PAID`, `SHIPPED` and `CANCELLED`, an exception `InvalidTransition`, and `Order` with `status` starting at `DRAFT`, `history` listing every status it has had, and `apply(action)` for `"submit"`, `"pay"`, `"ship"` and `"cancel"` (allowed from draft or submitted). Add `allowed_actions()` returning the sorted actions possible now.

checks.name: the happy path
checks.code:
order = Order()
for action in ["submit", "pay", "ship"]:
    order.apply(action)
assert order.status == Status.SHIPPED, order.status
want = [Status.DRAFT, Status.SUBMITTED, Status.PAID, Status.SHIPPED]
assert order.history == want, order.history

checks.name: cancelling before payment
checks.code:
draft = Order()
draft.apply("cancel")
assert draft.status == Status.CANCELLED, draft.status
submitted = Order()
submitted.apply("submit")
submitted.apply("cancel")
assert submitted.history == [Status.DRAFT, Status.SUBMITTED, Status.CANCELLED], submitted.history

checks.name: no cancelling after payment
checks.code:
order = Order()
order.apply("submit")
order.apply("pay")
raised = False
try:
    order.apply("cancel")
except InvalidTransition:
    raised = True
assert raised, "cancelling a paid order should raise InvalidTransition"
assert order.status == Status.PAID, order.status
assert len(order.history) == 3, order.history

checks.name: skipped steps and unknown actions
allowed actions follow the state
checks.code:
order = Order()
assert order.allowed_actions() == ["cancel", "submit"], order.allowed_actions()
order.apply("submit")
assert order.allowed_actions() == ["cancel", "pay"], order.allowed_actions()
order.apply("pay")
order.apply("ship")
assert order.allowed_actions() == [], order.allowed_actions()

hints: Put the five allowed moves in one dict keyed by `(status, action)`. `apply` looks the pair up instead of branching on the action alone.
When the lookup finds nothing, raise `InvalidTransition` before touching `status` or `history`. Start `history` as `[Status.DRAFT]`.
`allowed_actions` is a query on the same table: `sorted(action for state, action in TRANSITIONS if state == self.status)`.
lessons.explanation:
The if-chain looked only at the action, so a paid order could be cancelled and a draft could be shipped. The rule is really about pairs of state and action, and a dict keyed by those pairs says exactly that.

Because `apply` and `allowed_actions` read the same table, the buttons a screen shows can never disagree with what the order accepts. Adding a state, such as refunded, is one more line in the table.

lessons.title: The repository pattern
lessons.body:
# The repository pattern

The domain should not care whether products live in a dict, a sqlite file or a remote service. A repository hides storage behind a small collection-like interface: add an object, get it back by key, list them all.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Product:
    sku: str
    stock: int

class MemoryRepo:
    def __init__(self):
        self._rows = {}

    def add(self, product):
        self._rows[product.sku] = product

    def get(self, sku):
        return self._rows.get(sku)

repo = MemoryRepo()
repo.add(Product("MUG", 3))
print(repo.get("MUG"))
```

Services receive a repository as an argument. Tests pass the in-memory one, and the application passes one backed by a database:

```python
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute(
    "CREATE TABLE products (sku TEXT"
    " PRIMARY KEY, stock INT)")
db.execute(
    "INSERT INTO products VALUES (?, ?)",
    ("MUG", 3))
rows = db.execute("SELECT * FROM products")
print(rows.fetchall())
```

Both must behave the same, so write one contract test and run it against every implementation.
lessons.task: Write `SqliteProductRepository(conn)` matching `InMemoryProductRepository`: it creates a `products` table, `add(product)` inserts or replaces, `get(sku)` returns a new `Product` or `None`, and `list()` returns every product sorted by sku. Then fix the in-memory repository so that, like a database, it stores and returns copies.

checks.name: contract: add and get
checks.code:
import sqlite3
for repo in [InMemoryProductRepository(), SqliteProductRepository(sqlite3.connect(":memory:"))]:
    kind = type(repo).__name__
    repo.add(Product("MUG", 3))
    got = repo.get("MUG")
    assert got == Product("MUG", 3), (kind, got)
    assert repo.get("NOPE") is None, (kind, repo.get("NOPE"))

checks.name: contract: adding again replaces
checks.code:
import sqlite3
for repo in [InMemoryProductRepository(), SqliteProductRepository(sqlite3.connect(":memory:"))]:
    kind = type(repo).__name__
    repo.add(Product("MUG", 3))
    repo.add(Product("MUG", 1))
    got = repo.get("MUG")
    assert got == Product("MUG", 1), (kind, got)

checks.name: contract: list is sorted
checks.code:
import sqlite3
for repo in [InMemoryProductRepository(), SqliteProductRepository(sqlite3.connect(":memory:"))]:
    kind = type(repo).__name__
    for sku in ["PEN", "CUP", "MUG"]:
        repo.add(Product(sku, 1))
    got = repo.list()
    assert got == [Product("CUP", 1), Product("MUG", 1), Product("PEN", 1)], (kind, got)

checks.name: contract: stored products are copies
checks.code:
import sqlite3
for repo in [InMemoryProductRepository(), SqliteProductRepository(sqlite3.connect(":memory:"))]:
    kind = type(repo).__name__
    product = Product("MUG", 3)
    repo.add(product)
    product.stock = 0
    loaded = repo.get("MUG")
    loaded.stock = 99
    got = repo.get("MUG")
    assert got == Product("MUG", 3), (kind, "changes without add() leaked in", got)

checks.name: sqlite really stores rows
checks.code:
import sqlite3
conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
SqliteProductRepository(conn).add(Product("MUG", 2))
count = conn.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products").fetchone()[0]
assert count == 1, count
got = SqliteProductRepository(conn).get("MUG")
assert got == Product("MUG", 2), got

hints: Run the same steps against both repositories in your head: what does each return after `add`, after a second `add` of the same sku, and after you change an object you added?
`INSERT OR REPLACE` handles a repeated sku, `Product(*row)` turns a `(sku, stock)` row back into an object, and `ORDER BY sku` sorts.
In the in-memory repository, store `dataclasses.replace(product)` and return `replace(row)`, so callers never hold the stored object itself.
lessons.explanation:
The in-memory repository handed out the very object it stored, so a service that changed a product and forgot to save it would pass every test and then lose the change against a real database. A fake that is more forgiving than the real thing hides bugs; copying on the way in and out makes it as strict as sqlite.

Running one contract against every implementation is how you keep a fake honest. When a new implementation arrives, it gets the same tests for free.

lessons.title: A service layer
lessons.body:
# A service layer

A use case such as placing an order touches several things: it loads objects from a repository, asks the domain to change them, saves the result and reports back. A service function holds that orchestration, so web handlers, command-line tools and tests all call the same code.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Product:
    sku: str
    stock: int

    def restock(self, qty):
        if qty <= 0:
            raise ValueError(qty)
        self.stock += qty

def restock(repo, sku, qty):
    product = repo[sku]
    product.restock(qty)
    repo[sku] = product
    return product.stock

repo = {"MUG": Product("MUG", 1)}
print(restock(repo, "MUG", 4))
```

The service takes its repository as an argument and returns plain values. It does not parse requests, print or open connections; those belong to its callers. The rules live on the domain objects, so the service reads like a short list of steps.

Test a service with a fake repository built in the test. If the service works with that, the seam is real.
lessons.task: Write `Product.reserve(qty)` raising `OutOfStock` when `qty` is more than the stock. Write `place_order(repo, sku, qty)` that raises `ValueError` for a quantity below 1, `UnknownProduct` when `repo.get(sku)` is `None`, and otherwise reserves, saves with `repo.add(product)` and returns the remaining stock.

checks.name: reserving is a domain rule
checks.code:
product = Product("MUG", 5)
product.reserve(2)
assert product.stock == 3, product.stock
raised = False
try:
    product.reserve(4)
except OutOfStock:
    raised = True
assert raised, "reserving more than the stock should raise OutOfStock"
assert product.stock == 3, product.stock

checks.name: the service saves through the repository it is given
unknown products
out of stock saves nothing
bad quantities are refused first

hints: Move the stock rule into `Product.reserve`, so it holds wherever a product is changed. The service only calls it.
The service's steps: validate `qty`, `repo.get(sku)`, raise `UnknownProduct` for `None`, `product.reserve(qty)`, `repo.add(product)`, return the stock.
`reserve` raises `OutOfStock` before subtracting, when `qty > self.stock`. Check `qty < 1` at the top of `place_order`, before touching the repository.
lessons.explanation:
The starter changed the product in memory and returned, which looks right in a test that reads the same object back, and saves nothing to a real database. Saving through the repository makes the write visible to the fake, so a test can prove it happened.

Keeping the stock rule on `Product` means a second use case, such as a bulk import, cannot forget it. The service stays thin: it coordinates, and the domain decides.

lessons.title: Unit of work
lessons.body:
# Unit of work

Some use cases change several things that must succeed or fail together. A unit of work groups those changes: the service makes them through it, and nothing is stored until `commit()`. Leaving the `with` block without committing throws the changes away.

```python
import copy

class UnitOfWork:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data

    def __enter__(self):
        self.work = copy.deepcopy(self.data)
        return self

    def __exit__(self, *exc_info):
        self.work = None

    def commit(self):
        self.data.update(self.work)

store = {"MUG": 3}
with UnitOfWork(store) as uow:
    uow.work["MUG"] = 0
print(store)  # no commit, still 3
```

The service never learns whether it is talking to a database transaction or a copied dict. It opens the unit of work, changes things through it, and commits once, as its last step. An exception halfway leaves everything as it was, because nothing was published.

A fake unit of work can also record that `commit()` was called, so a test can check that the service committed.
lessons.task: Write `InMemoryUnitOfWork(stock)`, where `stock` maps sku to quantity: entering `with` exposes a working copy as `.stock`, `commit()` writes the copy back into the original dict and sets `committed` to `True`, and leaving without a commit discards the changes. Write `transfer(uow, from_sku, to_sku, qty)` that moves stock between two skus all or nothing, raising `ValueError` when `from_sku` has too little.

checks.name: changes need a commit
checks.code:
store = {"A": 5}
uow = InMemoryUnitOfWork(store)
with uow:
    uow.stock["A"] = 1
assert store == {"A": 5}, store
assert uow.committed is False, uow.committed

checks.name: commit writes back
checks.code:
store = {"A": 5}
uow = InMemoryUnitOfWork(store)
with uow:
    uow.stock["A"] = 1
    uow.stock["B"] = 2
    uow.commit()
assert store == {"A": 1, "B": 2}, store
assert uow.committed is True, uow.committed

checks.name: an exception discards the changes
checks.code:
store = {"A": 5}
uow = InMemoryUnitOfWork(store)
raised = False
try:
    with uow:
        uow.stock["A"] = 0
        raise RuntimeError("boom")
except RuntimeError:
    raised = True
assert raised, "the exception should leave the with block"
assert store == {"A": 5}, store

checks.name: transfer moves stock
checks.code:
store = {"A": 5, "B": 1}
uow = InMemoryUnitOfWork(store)
transfer(uow, "A", "B", 3)
assert store == {"A": 2, "B": 4}, store
assert uow.committed, "transfer should commit"

checks.name: transfer is all or nothing
transfer refuses too little stock

hints: The unit of work must not hand out the original dict. Make a copy in `__enter__` and let the service work on that.
`commit()` copies the working dict back into the original (`clear()` then `update()` keeps the caller's dict object). `__exit__` just drops the copy, so anything uncommitted is gone.
In `transfer`, do everything inside `with uow:`, check `uow.stock[from_sku] < qty` before changing anything, and call `uow.commit()` as the last line.
lessons.explanation:
Writing straight into the shared dict meant that when the second step failed, the first had already happened: stock left one sku and arrived nowhere. Working on a copy and publishing it only in `commit()` turns the whole transfer into one step.

Committing explicitly, as the service's last line, is deliberate: the safe default is to lose changes, not to keep half of them. A sqlite version of the same class would call `conn.commit()` and `conn.rollback()`, and `transfer` would not change at all.

lessons.title: Domain events and handlers
lessons.task: Write `Product.reserve(qty)` that raises `ValueError` when there is too little stock and appends `OutOfStock(sku)` to `self.events` when the stock reaches 0. Write `MessageBus` with `subscribe(event_type, handler)` and `publish(events)`, calling handlers in subscription order and ignoring events nobody subscribed to, and `reserve_and_publish(product, qty, bus)` that reserves, then publishes and clears the product's events.

checks.name: selling the last item records an event
checks.code:
product = Product("MUG", 2)
product.reserve(1)
assert product.events == [], product.events
product.reserve(1)
assert product.events == [OutOfStock("MUG")], product.events

checks.name: handlers run in subscription order
checks.code:
bus = MessageBus()
seen = []
bus.subscribe(OutOfStock, lambda e: seen.append(("first", e.sku)))
bus.subscribe(OutOfStock, lambda e: seen.append(("second", e.sku)))
bus.publish([OutOfStock("PEN")])
assert seen == [("first", "PEN"), ("second", "PEN")], seen

checks.name: events nobody handles are ignored
checks.code:
class Restocked:
    pass

bus = MessageBus()
seen = []
bus.subscribe(OutOfStock, seen.append)
bus.publish([Restocked()])
assert seen == [], seen

checks.name: each bus has its own handlers
checks.code:
one, two = MessageBus(), MessageBus()
seen = []
one.subscribe(OutOfStock, seen.append)
two.publish([OutOfStock("CUP")])
assert seen == [], "a handler on one bus fired for another"

checks.name: events are published once
checks.code:
bus = MessageBus()
seen = []
bus.subscribe(OutOfStock, seen.append)
product = Product("MUG", 1)
reserve_and_publish(product, 1, bus)
assert seen == [OutOfStock("MUG")], seen
assert product.events == [], product.events
other = Product("PEN", 3)
reserve_and_publish(other, 1, bus)
assert seen == [OutOfStock("MUG")], seen

hints: `reserve` should only record: `self.events.append(OutOfStock(self.sku))` when the stock reaches 0. No printing and no bus.
Give each bus its own `self.handlers = {}` in `__init__`, and look handlers up with `.get(type(event), [])` so unhandled events pass quietly.
In `reserve_and_publish`, take the events and reset the list before publishing: `events, product.events = product.events, []`, then `bus.publish(events)`.
lessons.explanation:
A dict written in the class body is shared by every instance, so a handler subscribed on one bus fired on all the others. State that belongs to an object goes in `__init__`.

The entity now knows nothing about email or buses; it only remembers what happened. Clearing its list before publishing means the same event cannot be handled twice, even if a handler triggers more work. New reactions are new subscriptions, and `Product` never changes for them.

lessons.title: Commands and queries
lessons.body:
# Commands and queries

A method that changes state and also returns data is hard to reason about: calling it just to look is no longer safe. Keep the two apart. A command changes something and returns nothing. A query returns data and changes nothing, so it can run as often as you like.

```python
class Cart:
    def __init__(self):
        self._items = {}

    def add(self, sku, qty):  # command
        n = self._items.get(sku, 0)
        self._items[sku] = n + qty

    def count(self):  # query
        return sum(self._items.values())

cart = Cart()
cart.add("MUG", 2)
cart.add("PEN", 1)
print(cart.count())
```

At the application level the same split separates a write side, which runs commands through the domain, from a read side, which answers queries from data shaped for the screen. Commands become small dataclasses that name an intention, each handled in one place.

## Who chooses the id?

If adding returns nothing, how does the caller learn the new id? Let the caller choose it, for example with `uuid4()`, and put it in the command.
lessons.task: Write frozen dataclasses `AddTask(task_id, title)` and `CompleteTask(task_id)`, and `TaskList.execute(command)` that applies either one and returns `None`, raising `ValueError` for an id that already exists, `KeyError` for completing an unknown id and `TypeError` for anything else. Write the queries `open_titles()`, the titles not yet done in the order they were added, and `done_count()`.

checks.name: commands return nothing
checks.code:
tasks = TaskList()
got = tasks.execute(AddTask(1, "write"))
assert got is None, got
got = tasks.execute(CompleteTask(1))
assert got is None, got

checks.name: queries report the state
checks.code:
tasks = TaskList()
tasks.execute(AddTask(7, "plan"))
tasks.execute(AddTask(3, "build"))
tasks.execute(AddTask(5, "ship"))
tasks.execute(CompleteTask(3))
assert tasks.open_titles() == ["plan", "ship"], tasks.open_titles()
assert tasks.done_count() == 1, tasks.done_count()

checks.name: queries change nothing
checks.code:
tasks = TaskList()
tasks.execute(AddTask(1, "plan"))
first = tasks.open_titles()
first.append("sneaky")
assert tasks.open_titles() == ["plan"], tasks.open_titles()
assert tasks.done_count() == 0, tasks.done_count()

checks.name: ids belong to the caller
checks.code:
tasks = TaskList()
tasks.execute(AddTask(1, "plan"))
raised = False
try:
    tasks.execute(AddTask(1, "again"))
except ValueError:
    raised = True
assert raised, "adding an existing id should raise ValueError"
assert tasks.open_titles() == ["plan"], tasks.open_titles()

checks.name: bad commands are refused

hints: `execute` should end without a `return` value. Callers that need data ask a query afterwards.
`match command:` with `case AddTask(task_id, title):` and `case CompleteTask(task_id):` dispatches by type; `case _:` catches anything else.
Refuse an `AddTask` whose id exists (`ValueError`) and a `CompleteTask` whose id does not (`KeyError`). Each query builds a new list or number from the stored data and never assigns to `self`.
lessons.explanation:
Returning the open titles from `execute` looked convenient, but every caller now pays for a query it may not want, and a command's result gets mixed up with its effect. With the caller choosing the id, a command needs no return value at all: the caller already knows how to refer to the new task.

Queries that only read can be cached, repeated and moved to a faster read store later. Commands that only write can be logged, retried and queued. Keeping them apart keeps those options open.

lessons.title: Ports and adapters
lessons.task: Write `HttpRates(client)` whose `rate(base, quote)` requests `GET /rates/{base}/{quote}`, raises for an error status, and returns the `"rate"` field as an exact `Decimal`, and `FakeRates(table)` reading a dict keyed by `(base, quote)`. Write `convert(amount, base, quote, rates)` returning the amount converted and rounded to cents, or the amount unchanged, without asking for a rate, when the currencies match.

checks.name: convert uses the port
checks.code:
from decimal import Decimal
rates = FakeRates({("EUR", "USD"): Decimal("1.1")})
got = convert(Decimal("10"), "EUR", "USD", rates)
assert got == Decimal("11.00"), got
got = convert(Decimal("3"), "EUR", "GBP", FakeRates({("EUR", "GBP"): Decimal("0.3333")}))
assert str(got) == "1.00", got

checks.name: the same currency needs no rate
the HTTP adapter calls the right path
checks.code:
import httpx
from decimal import Decimal
paths = []

def api(request):
    paths.append(request.url.path)
    return httpx.Response(200, json={"rate": "0.86"})

client = httpx.Client(base_url="https://rates.test", transport=httpx.MockTransport(api))
got = HttpRates(client).rate("USD", "EUR")
assert got == Decimal("0.86"), got
assert paths == ["/rates/USD/EUR"], paths

checks.name: JSON numbers become exact decimals
checks.code:
import httpx
from decimal import Decimal
client = httpx.Client(
    base_url="https://rates.test",
    transport=httpx.MockTransport(lambda request: httpx.Response(200, json={"rate": 1.1})),
)
got = HttpRates(client).rate("EUR", "USD")
assert isinstance(got, Decimal), type(got)
assert got == Decimal("1.1"), got

checks.name: an error status is not a rate
checks.code:
import httpx
client = httpx.Client(
    base_url="https://rates.test",
    transport=httpx.MockTransport(lambda request: httpx.Response(404, json={"detail": "unknown"})),
)
raised = False
try:
    HttpRates(client).rate("EUR", "XXX")
except httpx.HTTPStatusError:
    raised = True
assert raised, "a 404 should raise httpx.HTTPStatusError"

hints: `convert` should only talk to the port: one call to `rates.rate(base, quote)`, skipped when the currencies match. Round with `.quantize(Decimal("0.01"))`.
The adapter's job is translation. Call `response.raise_for_status()` before reading the body, and turn the JSON value into a `Decimal`.
A JSON number arrives as a float: `Decimal(str(value))` keeps `1.1` exact, where `Decimal(1.1)` would not.
lessons.explanation:
Returning `float` let the provider's representation leak into the domain, where money arithmetic needs exact decimals. The adapter is the one place that knows the wire format, so it is where JSON numbers become `Decimal` and HTTP failures become exceptions instead of bad data.

Because `HttpRates` receives its client, the test drives the real parsing code through an in-memory transport, and `convert` is tested with a three-line fake. Changing provider means writing one new adapter; `convert` stays exactly as it is.

lessons.title: Errors at layer boundaries
lessons.body:
# Errors at layer boundaries

Each layer should raise errors in its own vocabulary. A web handler should not catch `sqlite3.IntegrityError`, and the domain should not know HTTP status codes. At each boundary, catch what the inner layer raised and raise what the outer layer understands.

```python
import sqlite3

class EmailTaken(Exception):
    pass

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE users"
           " (email TEXT PRIMARY KEY)")

def add_user(email):
    try:
        db.execute("INSERT INTO users"
                   " VALUES (?)", (email,))
    except sqlite3.IntegrityError as err:
        raise EmailTaken(email) from err

add_user("ada@x.io")
try:
    add_user("ada@x.io")
except EmailTaken as err:
    print("taken:", err, "|", err.__cause__)
```

`from err` keeps the original exception as `__cause__`, so the traceback still shows the database error underneath.

## The outermost boundary

At the very edge, an error boundary turns known domain errors into responses, and anything unexpected into a generic failure. The details of that failure go to the logs, never to the user.
lessons.task: Write `SqliteUsers(conn)` whose `add(email)` raises `EmailTaken` chained from the `IntegrityError` and whose `get(email)` returns the email or raises `UserNotFound`. Write `handle(action, *args)` returning `(200, result)` on success, `(409, message)` for `EmailTaken`, `(404, message)` for `UserNotFound`, both messages naming the email, and `(500, "internal error")` for any other exception.

checks.name: a duplicate is a domain error
checks.code:
import sqlite3
users = SqliteUsers(sqlite3.connect(":memory:"))
users.add("ada@example.org")
caught = None
try:
    users.add("ada@example.org")
except EmailTaken as error:
    caught = error
assert caught is not None, "a second add should raise EmailTaken"
assert isinstance(caught.__cause__, sqlite3.IntegrityError), "chain it with raise ... from error"

checks.name: missing users
checks.code:
import sqlite3
users = SqliteUsers(sqlite3.connect(":memory:"))
users.add("bo@example.org")
assert users.get("bo@example.org") == "bo@example.org", users.get("bo@example.org")
raised = False
try:
    users.get("nobody@example.org")
except UserNotFound:
    raised = True
assert raised, "an unknown email should raise UserNotFound"

checks.name: the boundary maps errors to statuses
checks.code:
import sqlite3
users = SqliteUsers(sqlite3.connect(":memory:"))
got = handle(users.add, "cy@example.org")
assert got == (200, None), got
got = handle(users.get, "cy@example.org")
assert got == (200, "cy@example.org"), got
status, _ = handle(users.add, "cy@example.org")
assert status == 409, status
status, _ = handle(users.get, "zed@example.org")
assert status == 404, status

checks.name: messages name the email
checks.code:
import sqlite3
users = SqliteUsers(sqlite3.connect(":memory:"))
users.add("eve@example.org")
_, message = handle(users.add, "eve@example.org")
assert "eve@example.org" in message, message
_, message = handle(users.get, "fay@example.org")
assert "fay@example.org" in message, message

checks.name: unexpected errors stay generic
checks.code:
def broken():
    raise RuntimeError("password=hunter2 in /srv/app/config.py")

got = handle(broken)
assert got == (500, "internal error"), got

hints: Wrap the `INSERT` in `try`, catch `sqlite3.IntegrityError`, and `raise EmailTaken(email) from error`. In `get`, raise `UserNotFound(email)` when the row is `None`.
In `handle`, order matters: the `except` clauses for the domain errors come first, and a final `except Exception` comes last.
The last clause returns the fixed `(500, "internal error")`, never `str(error)`, which could reveal paths, SQL or data.
lessons.explanation:
Letting `IntegrityError` escape forces every caller to know that users live in sqlite, and the boundary could only answer 500 to an ordinary duplicate. Translating it in the adapter gives the rest of the code one meaningful error, and `from error` keeps the cause for whoever reads the traceback.

The outermost boundary is the only place that catches everything. It answers with a fixed message because exception text is written for developers and may contain secrets; in a real application that clause also logs the full traceback.

lessons.title: Caching behind an interface
lessons.task: Write `CachedPrices(inner, ttl, clock)` whose `price(sku)` calls `inner.price(sku)` only when there is no entry for `sku` or the entry is at least `ttl` seconds old by `clock()`, and whose `invalidate(sku)` drops one entry, ignoring unknown skus. A price of 0 is cached like any other.

checks.name: repeats come from memory
checks.code:
class Counting:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value, self.calls = value, []

    def price(self, sku):
        self.calls.append(sku)
        return self.value

inner = Counting(5)
cache = CachedPrices(inner, ttl=60, clock=lambda: 100.0)
assert cache.price("A") == 5, cache.price("A")
assert cache.price("A") == 5, cache.price("A")
cache.price("B")
cache.price("A")
assert inner.calls == ["A", "B"], inner.calls

checks.name: entries expire after ttl seconds
checks.code:
class Counting:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value, self.calls = value, []

    def price(self, sku):
        self.calls.append(sku)
        return self.value

now = [100.0]
inner = Counting(5)
cache = CachedPrices(inner, ttl=60, clock=lambda: now[0])
cache.price("A")
now[0] = 159.0
cache.price("A")
assert inner.calls == ["A"], ("still fresh at 59 seconds", inner.calls)
now[0] = 160.0
cache.price("A")
assert inner.calls == ["A", "A"], ("stale at 60 seconds", inner.calls)

checks.name: zero is a price too
checks.code:
class Counting:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value, self.calls = value, []

    def price(self, sku):
        self.calls.append(sku)
        return self.value

inner = Counting(0)
cache = CachedPrices(inner, ttl=60, clock=lambda: 0.0)
assert cache.price("FREE") == 0, cache.price("FREE")
cache.price("FREE")
assert inner.calls == ["FREE"], inner.calls

checks.name: invalidate drops one entry
checks.code:
class Counting:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value, self.calls = value, []

    def price(self, sku):
        self.calls.append(sku)
        return self.value

inner = Counting(5)
cache = CachedPrices(inner, ttl=60, clock=lambda: 0.0)
cache.price("A")
cache.price("B")
cache.invalidate("A")
cache.invalidate("NEVER-SEEN")
cache.price("A")
cache.price("B")
assert inner.calls == ["A", "B", "A"], inner.calls

checks.name: callers cannot tell the difference

hints: Store each entry with the time it was fetched, `(value, now)`, where `now = self.clock()`.
Refetch when there is no entry or `now - fetched_at >= self.ttl`. Test for a missing entry with `is None`, not truthiness, so a cached 0 still counts.
`invalidate` is `self._entries.pop(sku, None)`, which ignores skus that were never cached.
lessons.explanation:
`if not self.cache.get(sku)` treats a cached 0 like a missing entry, and without timestamps nothing ever expires. Storing the fetch time next to the value answers both.

The clock is a dependency like any other. Passed in, it lets a test move time by assigning a number, so the expiry rule is checked exactly at 59 and 60 seconds, instantly. And because the wrapper has the same `price` method, it can be added or removed where the application is wired together without touching a single caller.

lessons.title: Plugin registries
lessons.task: Write `Registry` with `register(name)`, a decorator that returns the function unchanged and raises `ValueError` if the name is taken, `get(name)` raising a `LookupError` whose message lists the available names, and `names()` returning them sorted. Register `"csv"` and `"json"` exporters on a module-level `exporters` registry and write `export(fmt, rows)` using it.

checks.name: registering keeps the function
names are sorted
checks.code:
registry = Registry()
registry.register("pdf")(lambda rows: "")
registry.register("csv")(lambda rows: "")
assert registry.names() == ["csv", "pdf"], registry.names()

checks.name: taken names are refused
checks.code:
registry = Registry()
registry.register("csv")(lambda rows: "first")
raised = False
try:
    registry.register("csv")(lambda rows: "second")
except ValueError:
    raised = True
assert raised, "registering csv twice should raise ValueError"
assert registry.get("csv")([]) == "first", registry.get("csv")([])

checks.name: unknown names list the choices
checks.code:
registry = Registry()
registry.register("pdf")(lambda rows: "")
registry.register("csv")(lambda rows: "")
message = None
try:
    registry.get("xml")
except LookupError as error:
    message = str(error)
assert message is not None, "an unknown name should raise LookupError"
assert "csv" in message and "pdf" in message, message

checks.name: the exporters registry
checks.code:
assert exporters.names() == ["csv", "json"], exporters.names()
got = export("csv", [["a", "b"], ["c", "d"]])
assert got == "a,b\nc,d", got
got = export("json", [["a"]])
assert got == '[["a"]]', got

checks.name: registries are independent
checks.code: assert Registry().names() == [], Registry().names()

hints: A decorator must return the function, or the decorated name becomes `None`. Check whether the name is taken inside `decorator`, before storing.
`get` can catch the `KeyError` and raise `LookupError(f"unknown {name!r}; available: ...")`, built from `self.names()`.
Register the JSON exporter just like CSV, with `@exporters.register("json")` returning `json.dumps(rows)`, so `export` is only `exporters.get(fmt)(rows)`.
lessons.explanation:
The starter's inner function returned nothing, so `@exporters.register("csv")` replaced `to_csv` with `None`: registration worked, but the module lost its own function. And `export` still special-cased JSON, which is the `if` chain the registry was meant to remove.

Refusing a taken name turns a silent override, where whichever plugin loads last wins, into an error at start-up. A `LookupError` that lists the choices turns a typo in a config file into a one-line fix.

lessons.title: Configuration and wiring
lessons.body:
# Configuration and wiring

A function that reads `os.environ` deep inside is configured by a global: tests have to patch it, and nobody can see which settings exist. Read configuration once, at start-up, into a frozen object, and pass it to whatever needs it.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Settings:
    db_path: str = ":memory:"
    page_size: int = 20

    @classmethod
    def from_env(cls, env):
        path = env.get("DB", ":memory:")
        size = env.get("PAGE_SIZE", "20")
        return cls(path, int(size))

print(Settings.from_env({"PAGE_SIZE": "5"}))
```

`from_env` takes any mapping, so a test passes a plain dict and the program passes `os.environ`.

## The composition root

One function near `main` builds the whole object graph: it creates the adapters and services and connects them. It is the only place that names the concrete classes, and its keyword arguments let a test swap any piece for a fake. This is dependency injection without a framework.
lessons.task: Write a frozen `Settings(db_path, page_size)` with `from_env(env)` reading `SHOP_DB` (default `":memory:"`) and `SHOP_PAGE_SIZE` (default 20), raising a `ValueError` that names the variable when the size is not a positive whole number. Write `build_app(settings, repo=None)` returning an `App` whose `repo` is the one given or a new `SqliteRepo(settings.db_path)`, and whose `catalog` is a `Catalog` sharing that repo with the configured page size.

checks.name: settings come from the mapping given
checks.code:
settings = Settings.from_env({"SHOP_DB": "shop.db", "SHOP_PAGE_SIZE": "5"})
assert (settings.db_path, settings.page_size) == ("shop.db", 5), settings
defaults = Settings.from_env({})
assert (defaults.db_path, defaults.page_size) == (":memory:", 20), defaults

checks.name: bad page sizes name the variable
settings are frozen
checks.code:
import dataclasses
settings = Settings.from_env({})
frozen = False
try:
    settings.page_size = 1
except dataclasses.FrozenInstanceError:
    frozen = True
assert frozen, "Settings should be a frozen dataclass"

checks.name: the wiring ignores os.environ
checks.code:
import os
os.environ["SHOP_PAGE_SIZE"] = "7"
app = build_app(Settings.from_env({"SHOP_PAGE_SIZE": "3"}))
del os.environ["SHOP_PAGE_SIZE"]
assert app.catalog.page_size == 3, app.catalog.page_size

checks.name: tests can swap the repository
checks.code:
class FakeRepo:
    def names(self):
        return ["cup", "mug", "pen"]

fake = FakeRepo()
app = build_app(Settings(page_size=2), repo=fake)
assert app.repo is fake, app.repo
assert app.catalog.repo is fake, "the catalog should use the repository passed in"
assert app.catalog.page(2) == ["pen"], app.catalog.page(2)

checks.name: the default wiring shares one repository
checks.code:
app = build_app(Settings.from_env({"SHOP_PAGE_SIZE": "2"}))
for name in ["pen", "cup", "mug"]:
    app.repo.add(name)
assert app.catalog.page(1) == ["cup", "mug"], app.catalog.page(1)
assert app.catalog.page(2) == ["pen"], app.catalog.page(2)

hints: `from_env` reads only the mapping it is given, with `env.get(name, default)`. Validate the page size text before converting it, and put the variable's name in the error.
In `build_app`, create the repository once, `if repo is None: repo = SqliteRepo(settings.db_path)`, and hand that same object to `Catalog`.
Pass `settings.page_size` to `Catalog` instead of any module-level constant, and return `App(settings=settings, repo=repo, catalog=Catalog(repo, settings.page_size))`.
lessons.explanation:
The module-level `PAGE_SIZE` was read once at import, before any test could choose a value, and building a second `SqliteRepo` gave the catalog its own empty in-memory database. Both bugs come from parts finding their own dependencies instead of receiving them.

With one composition root, the whole graph is visible in a few lines, `os.environ` is read in exactly one place, and a test builds the real application with a single fake swapped in. A dependency injection framework automates this wiring; for most Python applications, a plain function is enough.
